                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)

Forests with similar canopy heights can have different size distributions
within the same species. Management history, disturbance, and growing
conditions can leave patterns that canopy height alone does not explain.
We extend the [full plot-sampling model](full-model-plot-sampling.html) by
adding a spatial factor to diameter at breast height (DBH) allocation within
species. Magnitude and species allocation remain regression-only models.

The [preceding spatial article](spatial-effects-plot-sampling.html) placed
spatial effects in magnitude and species allocation. Here we show how the
same machinery describes variation in the conditional DBH distributions.
We explain the generating model, fit it, compare parameters and combined
intercept maps with truth, and summarize forest and stand densities.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**Example data**

[Download the conditional DBH-example data (ZIP)](downloads/conditional-dbh-plot-sampling.zip){.btn .btn-primary download="conditional-dbh-plot-sampling.zip"}

Extract it and use the folder containing `data/` as your R working directory.
The archive includes the generated population, its true parameters and
spatial factor, and `generate_population.R` to reproduce it with seed 1.
Generating the population again is optional.
:::

## Read the generated population

This example uses the same forest, 151 sampled plots, 4,812 prediction cells,
and standardized canopy-height predictor `x` as the
[data article](plot-sampling-data.html), with new simulated counts.
We read the data and the generating parameters. Coordinates ending in
`_km` are in kilometers; the polygons and original coordinates are in meters.

```{r}
#| label: read-data

library(magComp)
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)

plots <- read_csv("data/plots.csv")

prediction <- read_csv("data/prediction.csv")

dbh_parameters <- read_csv("data/dbh_parameters.csv")

true_parameters <- read_csv("data/true_parameters.csv", na = "NA")

forest <- st_read("data/forest.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)

prediction_cells <- st_read("data/prediction_cells.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)

plot_locations <- st_read("data/plot_locations.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)

cell_stand_areas <- read_csv("data/cell_stand_areas.csv")

species_order <- c("pine", "oak", "birch")
dbh_classes <- c("10-20", "20-30", "30-40", "40-50", "50+")
```

The count columns describe the 15 species-by-DBH categories. The `w` column
holds the true spatial factor score at each location, for comparison after
fitting. It is not supplied as a covariate.

## A shared factor for within-species size distributions

Let $a$ index species and $b$ index DBH class. The leading allocation assigns
trees to species with probabilities $q_{ia}$. Within species $a$, the child
allocation assigns them to DBH classes with probabilities $r_{ib\mid a}$.
Their product $p_{iab}=q_{ia}r_{ib\mid a}$ gives the probability of belonging
to species $a$ and DBH class $b$.

As in the earlier articles, we allocate trees through the DBH classes in
order. Among trees not already assigned to a smaller class, the probability
of entering class $b$ is

$$
\pi_{iab}^{(B\mid A)}=
\Phi\left\{\alpha_{0,ab}^{(B\mid A)}+
\alpha_{1,ab}^{(B\mid A)}x_i+
\lambda_{ab}^{(B\mid A)}w^{(B\mid A)}(\mathbf{s}_i)\right\},
\qquad b=1,\ldots,4,
$$

where $\Phi$ is the standard Normal distribution function. Each species
has four allocation steps; its fifth class receives the remaining trees.
The class probabilities are
$r_{ib\mid a}=\pi_{iab}^{(B\mid A)}\prod_{h<b}(1-\pi_{iah}^{(B\mid A)})$
for the first four classes, with the remaining probability assigned to `50+`.

There is **one spatial factor score at each location**, shared by all 12
species-by-DBH allocation steps. Each step has its own loading
$\lambda_{ab}^{(B\mid A)}$. Thus a common pattern can affect pine, oak, and
birch differently, and can have different effects across their size classes.
The loading matrix stacks four rows for each species into a single
12-by-1 matrix. These are not separate factors for each species.

The factor has mean zero, variance one, and exponential correlation
$\exp\{-\phi_w\|\mathbf{s}-\mathbf{s}'\|\}$. We use $\phi_w=3$, so its
correlation falls to approximately 0.05 at 1 km. The loadings determine the
scale and direction of each DBH effect. We choose `pine:10-20` as the anchor
row and constrain its loading to be positive when fitting; its value is
estimated along with the other loadings.

The generating coefficients and loadings are given below. A positive factor
score increases pine's and birch's probabilities of allocation to the first
class, while decreasing oak's. Because later steps act on the remaining
trees, a loading describes a conditional allocation, not a change in the
overall proportion of that class.

```{r}
#| label: generating-coefficients

knitr::kable(dbh_parameters, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("Species", "DBH class", "Intercept", "Slope", "Loading"))
```

Magnitude uses $\log M_i=\log(350)-0.2x_i$ and
$N_i\mid M_i,r_M\sim\operatorname{NB}(a_iM_i,r_M)$ with size $r_M=50$.
Species allocation uses the same canopy-height regressions as the
[full-model article](full-model-plot-sampling.html).
Neither component has a random effect in this population. We also leave
smoothing across DBH classes out of this example.

### Generate the population

We generate the factor jointly over the plots and prediction cells from a
full Gaussian process (GP). Given that field, we draw total counts, allocate
them among species, and allocate each species count among DBH classes.
The supplied files contain these completed steps. The optional code below
comes from `generate_population.R`; running that script reproduces them.
Full-GP generation requires more memory than reading the supplied files.

## Fit the conditional spatial model

We arrange the sampled counts into one row per plot, species, and DBH class.
This is the same data structure as for the full model.

```{r}
#| label: model-data

trees <- plots |>
  select(plot_id, area, x, easting_km, northing_km, contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(contains(":"), names_to = c("species", "dbh_class"),
               names_sep = ":", values_to = "count") |>
  mutate(
    species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
    dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes)
  ) |>
  arrange(plot_id, species, dbh_class)

dat <- magCompData(
  trees,
  unit = plot_id, categories = c(species, dbh_class),
  tree_count = count, design = fixedArea(area)
)
```

We approximate the GP with a 15-neighbor nearest-neighbor Gaussian process
(NNGP) [@datta2016nngp]. The `factor_nngp()` term belongs in
`dbh_class | species`, so it modifies DBH allocation within species.
`factor_names = "size"` labels this factor in the parameter output.

```{r}
#| label: fit

fit <- magComp(
  dat,
  magnitude = ~ x,
  composition = magCompComposition(
    species ~ x,
    dbh_class | species ~ x +
      factor_nngp(easting_km, northing_km, K = 1, m = 15,
                   anchors = "pine:10-20", factor_names = "size", name = "space")
  ),
  control = magCompControl(
    n_samples = 50000,
    n_burn = 20000,
    n_thin = 10,
    n_chains = 3,
    n_cores = 3,
    chain_seeds = 1:3,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
)
```

The conditional DBH factor can be harder to estimate than a species-allocation
factor because it has more loadings and relies on smaller within-species counts,
especially in later DBH classes. We therefore use longer chains here.

Each chain runs for 50,000 iterations. We discard the first 20,000 and retain
every tenth draw, giving 3,000 retained draws per chain.
The model estimates the DBH factor's decay and loadings using default priors
and automatic starting values. Negative-binomial size is also estimated
because the magnitude model has no random effect.

## Compare parameters and inspect mixing

We first compare the magnitude and species coefficients, size, and spatial
decay with their generating values. The remaining parameters describe the
conditional DBH model and are plotted below.

```{r}
#| label: parameter-summary

parameter_summary <- summary(fit)

parameter_summary |>
  inner_join(true_parameters, by = c("component", "block", "parameter", "index")) |>
  select(symbol, truth, mean, q2_5, q97_5, rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               col.names = c("Parameter", "Truth", "Mean", "2.5%", "97.5%", "R-hat", "ESS"))
```

The decay is estimated below its generating value in this realization,
corresponding to longer spatial dependence. Its chains agree well, but the
95% interval does not include the generating value. Good chain agreement
does not guarantee that an interval contains the truth; a single simulated
forest does not establish interval coverage.

We match each DBH coefficient or loading to its generating value. The index
identifies species, DBH allocation step, and either a regression coefficient
or the named factor.

```{r}
#| label: dbh-parameter-comparison

dbh_truth <- dbh_parameters |>
  pivot_longer(c(intercept, slope, loading), names_to = "coefficient", values_to = "truth") |>
  mutate(
    parameter = if_else(coefficient == "loading", "loadings", "coefficients"),
    index = paste(species, dbh_class,
                   recode(coefficient, intercept = "(Intercept)", slope = "x", loading = "size"),
                   sep = ":")
  )

dbh_comparison <- parameter_summary |>
  filter(block == "dbh_class|species") |>
  inner_join(dbh_truth, by = c("parameter", "index")) |>
  mutate(
    species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
    dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes[1:4]),
    coefficient = factor(coefficient, levels = c("intercept", "slope", "loading"),
                          labels = c("Intercept", "Slope", "Loading"))
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-dbh-parameters
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "DBH regression coefficients and spatial loadings. Blue points and bars show posterior means and 95% credible intervals; black marks show generating values. Each column describes one species, with four allocation steps."

ggplot(dbh_comparison, aes(dbh_class, mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0.15, color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(aes(shape = "Estimate"), color = "#0072B2", size = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = truth, shape = "Truth"), size = 5) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Truth" = 95, "Estimate" = 16),
                     breaks = c("Truth", "Estimate"), name = NULL) +
  facet_grid(coefficient ~ species, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "DBH allocation step (cm)", y = "Parameter value") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The larger loadings are positive for pine and birch and negative for oak,
as specified in the population. Later birch classes contain fewer trees and
have wider intervals. We summarize chain agreement separately for the DBH
intercepts, slopes, and loadings.

```{r}
#| label: separate-diagnostics
dbh_comparison |>
  group_by(coefficient) |>
  summarise(max_rhat = max(rhat), min_ess = min(ess), .groups = "drop") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               col.names = c("Coefficient", "Largest R-hat", "Smallest ESS"))
```

The slopes and loadings have R-hats close to one, while the separate
intercepts mix slowly despite the longer chains. An intercept and the factor
contribution can trade off while leaving their sum nearly unchanged. In
traceplots, the intercepts and average factor contribution would move in
opposite directions while their sums remain more stable.

For DBH step $b$ within species $a$, that combined intercept is
$\alpha_{0,ab}^{(B\mid A)}+\lambda_{ab}^{(B\mid A)}w^{(B\mid A)}(\mathbf{s}_i)$.
It describes allocation on the probit scale at average canopy height.
We check these sums averaged over the observed plot locations, using all
retained draws. The table reports the largest R-hat and smallest effective
sample size (ESS) across the four DBH steps for each species.

```{r}
#| label: combined-diagnostics

combined_diagnostics <- summary(fit, type = "combined", group = ".all")

combined_diagnostics |>
  group_by(parent) |>
  summarise(max_rhat = max(rhat), min_ess = min(ess), .groups = "drop") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               col.names = c("Species", "Largest R-hat", "Smallest ESS"))
```

The averaged combined intercepts have R-hats near one and much larger ESS.
These diagnostics describe the sums; the separate intercept summaries retain
their mixing limitations. The maps below show the combined intercepts, which
enter the allocation probabilities directly.

## Predict across the forest

We predict all cells together, retaining 100 draws per chain. Each draw
includes a spatial factor realization conditional on the fitted effects
and previously generated prediction effects. The observation target then
generates total counts and their species-by-DBH allocations; `type = "density"`
divides those counts by each cell's area. We keep the same latent draws for
the combined-intercept maps.

```{r}
#| label: predict

set.seed(1)

predictions <- predict(
  fit,
  prediction |> select(plot_id, x, area, easting_km, northing_km),
  type = "density",
  target = "observation",
  n_draws = 100,
  summary = "samples",
  keep_effects = TRUE
)
```

### Map the first DBH allocation step

We map the combined intercept for the 10–20 cm class in each species.
Higher values mean a greater probability of entering this class at average
canopy height. The three maps share one spatial factor but differ through
their intercepts and loadings.

```{r}
#| label: map-values

intercept_summary <- summary(samples(predictions, type = "combined")) |>
  filter(stick %in% paste(species_order, "10-20", sep = ":")) |>
  transmute(plot_id = as.integer(unit), species = parent, Estimate = mean)

true_intercepts <- prediction |>
  select(plot_id, w) |>
  cross_join(filter(dbh_parameters, dbh_class == "10-20")) |>
  transmute(plot_id, species, Truth = intercept + loading * w)

map_values <- intercept_summary |>
  left_join(true_intercepts, by = c("plot_id", "species")) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Truth, Estimate), names_to = "source", values_to = "intercept") |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
         source = factor(source, levels = c("Truth", "Estimate")))

intercept_maps <- prediction_cells |>
  left_join(map_values, by = "plot_id", relationship = "many-to-many")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-dbh-intercepts
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-cap: "True and estimated combined intercepts for the 10–20 cm DBH allocation step within each species, on a common probit scale. White circles mark sampled plots."

ggplot(intercept_maps) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = intercept), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = forest, fill = NA, color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = plot_locations, shape = 21, fill = "white", size = 0.7, stroke = 0.2) +
  facet_grid(species ~ source) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Combined\nintercept\n(probit)") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void()
```

Opposite loading signs give oak a different spatial pattern from pine and
birch. Posterior means smooth over uncertainty between sampled plots;
the predictive samples retain that uncertainty when summarizing densities.

## Compare forest and stand densities with truth

We use the same area-weighted aggregation as in the previous articles.
`standSummary()` combines the predictive densities into one forest density
per species-by-DBH category in each draw.

```{r}
#| label: forest-summary

forest_predictions <- standSummary(
  predictions,
  data = prediction,
  unit = plot_id,
  represented_area = area,
  summary = "samples"
)

forest_truth <- prediction |>
  select(contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "category", values_to = "count") |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(truth = sum(count) / sum(prediction$area), .groups = "drop")

forest_comparison <- summary(forest_predictions) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(forest_truth, by = "category") |>
  separate_wider_delim(category, delim = ":", names = c("species", "dbh_class")) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
         dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest-distributions
#| fig-cap: "Forest species-by-DBH densities. Blue points and bars show posterior predictive means and 95% intervals; black marks show simulated truth."

ggplot(forest_comparison, aes(dbh_class, mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0.15, color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(aes(shape = "Estimate"), color = "#0072B2", size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y = truth, shape = "Truth"), size = 6) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Truth" = 95, "Estimate" = 16),
                     breaks = c("Truth", "Estimate"), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ species, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "DBH class (cm)", y = "Trees per hectare") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

For stands, we supply the cell–stand area table from the
[data article](plot-sampling-data.html#cell-areas-within-stands).
Both truth and prediction use a cell's density in every intersected stand,
weighted by the area of that intersection.

```{r}
#| label: stand-summary

stand_predictions <- standSummary(
  predictions,
  data = cell_stand_areas,
  unit = prediction_id,
  group = stand_id,
  represented_area = area_ha,
  summary = "samples"
)

stand_truth <- prediction |>
  select(plot_id, area, contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(contains(":"), names_to = "category", values_to = "count") |>
  inner_join(cell_stand_areas, by = c("plot_id" = "prediction_id"),
              relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  group_by(stand_id, category) |>
  summarise(truth = weighted.mean(count / area, area_ha), .groups = "drop")

stand_comparison <- summary(stand_predictions) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  rename(stand_id = unit) |>
  left_join(stand_truth, by = c("stand_id", "category")) |>
  separate_wider_delim(category, delim = ":", names = c("species", "dbh_class")) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, levels = species_order))

stand_limits <- stand_comparison |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(limit = max(truth, mean, q97_5), .groups = "drop")
```

Each point below is one species-by-DBH density in one of the 249 stands.
Prediction combines canopy height, the shared spatial factor, and its
species-by-DBH loadings before aggregation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stand-densities
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "Estimated versus true species-by-DBH densities across stands. Faint bars show 95% posterior predictive intervals; dashed lines mark equality. Axes have matching limits within each species panel."

ggplot(stand_comparison, aes(truth, mean)) +
  geom_blank(data = stand_limits, aes(x = limit, y = limit)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0,
                color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", size = 0.9, alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ species, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "True density (trees/ha)", y = "Estimated density (trees/ha)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)
```

## A stratum alternative

If within-species size distributions vary among known groups of stands, we
can replace the spatial factor with a stratum factor. With units assigned
to strata as in the [stratum article](stratum-effects-plot-sampling.html),
the composition specification would be

```{r}
#| label: stratum-alternative

stratum_composition <- magCompComposition(
  species ~ x,
  dbh_class | species ~ x +
    factor_iid(stratum_id, K = 1, anchors = "pine:10-20",
                 factor_names = "size", name = "stratum")
)
```

This specifies a separate model to fit to data containing `stratum_id`.
One unit-variance score is shared within each stratum, and the 12 loading
rows again allow different responses among species and DBH allocation steps.
The spatial model instead shares information through distance. Either
choice uses the same `predict()` and `standSummary()` workflow.

The [space-time article](space-time-effects-plot-sampling.html) turns to
repeated plot measurements, adding temporal dependence to spatial effects
in magnitude and species allocation.
